entries.title: 9 Windows Laptops That Give MacBooks a Run for Their Money
entries.summary: Windows laptops have never been so good, and they’re only going to get better as we move through 2026.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The fight between MacBooks and Windows laptops has never been tighter. There are now more competent alternatives to every MacBook in the lineup. Whether you're choosing Windows because you don't use Apple, you need it for certain software, or just because you like the variety of hardware options, there are tons of great Windows laptops to choose from right now.

I've already tested dozens of Windows laptops this year, and have been reviewing laptops for over a decade. These are my recommendations you can buy right now, including many that were recently refreshed.

For more laptop recommendations, check out our Best 2-in-1 Laptops, Best Gaming Laptops, and Best Budget Laptops. Meanwhile, our overall Best Laptops guide includes the Best Chromebooks and Best MacBooks, too. Still unsure? Read our guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop.

Updated September 2026: I've added the Dell XPS 13, HP OmniBook 5, HP OmniBook Ultra, Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x, and Alienware 15. I've also moved some older picks to the honorable mentions section at the bottom.

Compare Top 9 Windows Laptops

Display CPU GPU RAM Storage Thickness (inches) Weight (pounds)
Dell XPS 13 13.4-inch, 2560 x 1600 (IPS) Intel Core 5 320 Arc 8 GB, 16 GB 512 GB 0.5 2.2
HP OmniBook 5 14 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 (OLED) Qualcomm Snapdragon X Adreno 16 GB 512 GB 0.5 2.8
Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x 14-inch, 2560 x 1600 (IPS) Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus Adreno 16 GB 512 GB 0.61 3.1
HP OmniBook Ultra 14 14-inch, 2880 x 1800 (OLED) Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus Adreno 16 GB, 32 GB 512 GB, 1 TB 0.42 2.8
Dell XPS 14 16-inch, 2880 x 1800 (OLED) Intel Core Ultra X7 358H Arc B750 16 GB to 64 GB 512 GB to 4 TB 0.58 3
Asus Zenbook A14 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 (OLED) Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus Adreno 16 GB 512 GB 0.63 2.2
Framework Laptop 13 13.5-inch, 2256 x 1504 (IPS) AMD Ryzen AI 5 340 Radeon 16 GB, up to 96 GB 500 GB, up to 4 TB 0.62 2.9
Lenovo Yoga Pro 9i 16 Up to 3200 x 2000 (Tandem OLED) Intel Core Ultra 9 285H Up to Nvidia RTX 5070 32 GB 1 TB 0.7 4.3
Razer Blade 16 16-inch, 2560 x 1600 (OLED) AMD Ryzen AI 9 365 Up to Nvidia RTX 5090 16 GB, up to 64 GB 1 TB, up to 4 TB 0.69 4.7

Other Windows Laptops to Consider

Dell 14 Plus: This laptop sold for hundreds less throughout 2025. And yet, even at around $1,000, I still find it a really solid deal. I do think the XPS 13 is better in a number of ways, especially the display quality and sleek design. However, the extra ports on the Dell 14 Plus are handy, and some may appreciate the slightly larger screen. It also has an upper hand with twice the storage as the Dell XPS 13 and Surface Laptop 7th Edition.

Surface Laptop 7th Edition: I waited a long time for a Windows machine like this Surface Laptop, which came out in 2024—something that could truly compete with the MacBook Air, and it does. The Snapdragon X2 Elite version of the Surface Laptop is available and should provide extra performance. It’s much more expensive at $1,600, which feels overpriced. It occasionally drops to under $1,400, however, which is closer to what the original model sells for. One caveat: You might come across the Surface Laptop 13, which came out in 2025 and is cheaper. I haven't tested that one, but it lacks some of the features I like in the 7th Edition, such as the 3:2 screen.

Lenovo LOQ 15: For many months, the LOQ 15 (8/10, WIRED Recommended) was one of the only gaming laptops under $1,000 that came with an RTX 5060 graphics card. The price has since risen significantly. Yet, it's still a laptop I recommend, as others have also increased in price. And unlike other cheaper gaming laptops, the LOQ 15 has a higher-quality display that's both bright and colorful.

Alienware 15 Gaming Laptop: Speaking of cheaper gaming laptops, the Alienware 15 falls into many of those same traps. It's thick and chunky, yes, but it also has a lower-quality display than you might expect for the price. But it delivers decent performance, has a nice design, and offers the option of an RTX 5050 graphics card. However, the price has gone up by nearly $600.

Surface Pro 12: Unfortunately, if you're looking for a Windows tablet or 2-in-1, your options are slim. There's a newer Surface Pro 13.8 with one of the Snapdragon X2 chips, which are quite expensive. And the detachable keyboard cover (that you should absolutely buy) doesn't come bundled. That's why, at this point, the smaller (and now cheaper) Surface Pro 12 is what most people should buy.

Asus Zenbook S 16: Windows laptops haven't always been known for being lookers. The Asus Zenbook S 16 undoes that stereotype. This thing is absolutely gorgeous, and not in a way that tries to mimic the MacBook. It has its own aesthetic with its white "ceraluminum" material, and I love it. It's also remarkably thin, has an expansive touchpad, and a sharp OLED display—the complete package. The only problem is that the Zenbook S 16 is quite expensive, and prices haven't dropped as much as I hoped. For a smaller model, check out the Zenbook S 14, which is very similar, except it uses an Intel chip instead.

What to Look For in a Windows Laptop

You'll want to read our extensive guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop, but for the basics, decide what category of laptop you need. Most people should buy a 13-inch or 14-inch laptop, and spending around $750 to $1,000 is a good place to start. At this price, you should expect good battery life, a decent screen, solid performance for basic tasks, and a comfortable keyboard and touchpad. You should also expect at least 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Anything more than that gets into premium territory where you're paying for higher specs, more performance, or extra features. If you want a discrete GPU for gaming or creative workflows, you'll need to spend more.

A laptop like the Dell 14 Plus is a great example of what you can get in this price range. You can even find laptops with OLED panels and up to one terabyte of storage, depending on how good the discounts are. I would consider anything under $750 a cheap laptop, and it will come with significant compromises, especially in panel and touchpad quality. Fortunately, laptops that use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip get great battery life, even when they fall under $750, such as the HP OmniBook 5 14.

Here's a list of important specs to consider:

CPU: Thanks to the huge variety of good chip options, it's never been trickier to buy a laptop. For thin-and-light laptops, I would recommend one of the following chips:

  • Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Snapdragon X Plus, or Snapdragon X Elite
  • Qualcomm Snapdragon X2, Snapdragon X2 Plus, or Snapdragon X2 Elite
  • Intel Core Ultra 225 V or Core Ultra 7 258V
  • Intel Core 5 320, Core Ultra 7 365, or Core Ultra X7 358H

There are many variations of these chips, so you'll undoubtedly run across other strings of numbers, especially on the Intel front. But the above is a good place to start. There’s lots more to say in the world of gaming laptops or content creation devices, so make sure to read our full guide to How to Buy a Gaming Laptop.

GPU: As of now, Intel's Panther Lake X7 or X9 chips have the most powerful integrated graphics. You'll find them in laptops like the Dell XPS 14, which can replicate discrete GPU-level performance like the RTX 4050. Unlike many laptops with discrete GPUs, though, Panther Lake X chips offer great battery life, making them better Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro.

For discrete options, you'll want one of the latest Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs, such as the RTX 5060. The biggest leap in performance is between the RTX 5070 and the RTX 5070 Ti, which increases VRAM to 12 GB.

RAM (or memory): Stick with at least 16 GB if you can. Since the Copilot+ designation was introduced in 2024, it has become the new standard. You'll even find laptops as cheap as $600 that have 16 GB of memory. Gamers and content creators should upgrade to 32 GB if possible, though the ongoing memory shortage makes this more expensive. There's been a new surge in 8 GB options, such as the Dell XPS 13, but these should be reserved for only light usage.

Storage: Similar to memory, many laptops have moved to 512 GB as the new standard, and you'll find lots of affordable laptops with that as the base configuration. Upgrading to 1 or 2 terabytes, where possible, will make your life that much easier, especially since many laptops don't offer expandable storage.

Display: Laptops are usually categorized by screen size, with 13-inch, 14-inch, and 16-inch being the most common. Consider size, resolution, refresh rate, and panel type.

Portability: Aside from display size, chassis thickness and weight are the main factors, determining how portable a laptop is to travel with. Other dimensions are important too, but more often than not, that is determined by the screen size.

Ports: Many laptops are limited to USB-C and a headphone jack these days, with some exceptions that include USB-A or HDMI. Make sure your laptop has what you need, or you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station to add ports or increase external display support.

Windows 11 vs. Windows 10: What Are the Differences?

If you haven't heard, if you're still on Windows 10, you're no longer getting security updates—at least not without paying extra. If you're wondering what to expect in a new laptop that runs Windows 11, here's a breakdown of the major changes:

Interface: The Start Menu is now centered in the Taskbar and looks a bit different. Visually, it's quite different, but it still functions the same, offering you quick access to applications and documents. Beyond the Start Menu, just about every app will have a different visual flair, with rounded corners and a streamlined aesthetic. While you can still do what you could in Windows 10, things like Settings, Notifications, and System Tray will feel different. You'll also find a new Widgets tray you can activate on the left side of the Taskbar. Unfortunately, you can no longer move the Taskbar to a different side of the screen.

Hardware requirements: This is where most of the frustration around Windows 11 stems from. No one likes being forced to buy new hardware, and while requirements like having at least 4 GB of RAM or 64 GB of storage seem straightforward, the need for a security chip called TPM 2.0 has forced a lot of Windows 10 users to upgrade otherwise good motherboards and CPUs just to move to an operating system they didn't want to begin with.

Performance features: There are tons of new features that help Windows 11 play nicer with accessories and third-party software. One of my favorite examples is HDR support. Windows 11 finally fixes the HDR problem that made using a proper HDR monitor so troublesome, especially in games using Auto HDR. Speaking of games, Windows 11 has features like Game Mode, DirectStorage, and optimizations for windowed games, all of which make for a faster, smoother PC gaming experience.

Is Now a Good Time to Buy?

Laptop prices have been increasing all year, thanks to the memory shortage. In many cases, that means the same laptops cost hundreds of dollars more on any given day. For example, the Dell 14 Plus currently sells for around $1,000, which isn't a terrible price for the configuration. But it was consistently selling for between $650 and $750 for most of 2025. That said, I don't think prices will drop anytime soon. The future of memory pricing is unknown, but many analysts and manufacturers say it will at least last through next year and possibly into 2028.

So yes, there are tons of good options to choose from right now at reasonable prices. All the newest models with the latest chips from Intel, Qualcomm, and AMD are finally out in the wild, along with plenty of good options from 2025. You can always wait for a big sales event like Black Friday, but the savings on specific laptops may not be as big as you might assume. The only significant new hardware we're waiting to see later this year are the new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops. A lot is still unknown about these devices, but they are slated for a fall 2026 release window.

entries.title: Everything New You Can Do With Siri AI
entries.summary: When iOS 27 arrives, it will bring with it a fully revamped assistant for your iPhone.
entries.content:
Siri made its debut on the iPhone in 2011, five years ahead of Google Assistant and 11 years before ChatGPT would open up to the public. Despite the head start, Apple's voice AI has been comprehensively overtaken in recent years, and made to look rather primitive compared to the many generative AI rivals it’s now up against.

With the launch of iOS 27, Apple and Siri are fighting back. There's a new name—Siri AI—and a host of new capabilities that are coming to your iPhone.

These are the new features that you'll be able to make use of once iOS 27 appears on your handset, if you're running the iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max or later (including, of course, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo). Only these latest phones have the necessary on-board silicon to meet the higher AI processing demands.

Get More Personal Context

You'll notice when Siri AI arrives that it spends some time indexing everything on your iPhone. That's so it can dig deep into your texts, emails, calendars, and whatever else you have stored on your phone (everything is kept on-device though—nothing gets sent back to Apple).

It means you can ask natural questions about text conversations, email interactions, and appointments—"What day is my work appraisal happening?" for example, or "Where did I say I'd meet Mom?"—and get informed, personalized answers back, based on what's already stored in your apps.

This works for photos and videos as well. Open up the Photos app and you're able to ask Siri AI to show you all the pictures of your pet, or the images you took on your last vacation, or all the photos of trees you've collected, via simple, conversational prompts.

Ask About Anything on the Screen

Siri AI knows what you're looking at while you're using your iPhone—perhaps even better than you do. Whereas before you would've had to take a screenshot and give it to Siri to look at, now you can just ask.

So if you're on the web in Safari, you can say "Hey Siri" and then get it to summarize the text onscreen or identify a landmark in an image in an online article. You can ask what certain options mean in Settings, or look up more details about a game you're thinking about downloading from the App Store.

The same sort of visual processing is available through the iOS Camera app too: Just switch to Siri mode using the selector by the shutter button, and ask Siri AI about anything that's in view (nutritional information about an item on a menu, for instance).

Write and Edit Text Anywhere

The old Siri could generate text for you, but it offloaded the job to an integrated ChatGPT plug-in. With Siri AI, no third-party help is needed, and you can use it for things like text messages and emails.

Just call up Siri AI by saying "Hey Siri" or tapping on the Write with Siri link, then tell it what you want to say or describe the edits you'd like it to make. You can instruct it to make your messages sound more or less formal, to expand or shorten sections of text, or to turn quick notes into full paragraphs and sentences.

You retain final approval over what's written, and can continue to make manual or AI-generated edits as you go. Siri AI lets you review all the changes and jump backwards and forwards through your different revisions.

Do More Inside Your Apps

Not only can Siri AI access more information pulled from your apps, it can now take more actions inside these apps. You’re able to create calendar events or switch playlists just by talking or typing to the digital assistant.

Some of this was already possible with the earlier incarnation of Siri, but now you can go deeper and do more inside your apps, and you should be able to use a wider range of natural language prompts to get stuff done—just as if you were talking to a real human assistant you'd handed your phone over to.

You might see some suggestions for actions pop up as well—so if someone texts you a date and time, you’ll see Siri inviting you to create a calendar event. Over time, deeper hooks into third-party, non-Apple apps should show up too.

Get at All Your Chats With the Siri App

For the first time, Apple's digital AI assistant has its own app. Launch it from the home screen to access your Siri AI conversation history and sync your queries and requests across different Apple devices.

Compared to the likes of Claude, Gemini, or ChatGPT, this is something Siri AI has been sorely missing, and it gives you another way of launching chats with the assistant: Open up the dedicated app rather than invoking it with a voice command.

Also, look out for what Apple calls "broad world knowledge" in the new Siri AI. Roughly translated, stand-alone queries about the history of Rome or how to fix a leaky faucet should bring up more informed, complete responses in the app.

Customize Siri’s Pace and Expressivity

This final tip needs even more computing resources, so it’s only for the most powerful devices—the 2026 iPhones, as well as the iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, and iPhone Air—as far as iPhones go.

The actual feature is being able to adjust the tone, speed, and what Apple calls the "expressivity" of Siri AI's spoken responses to you. In other words, you can tweak the personality of the assistant to some extent, as well as switch between voices.

To find these new options, open up Settings on your iPhone and tap Siri. You can customize Siri AI in other ways from this same screen, including changing the AI’s default voice and choosing how long to keep chats stored in your history.

entries.title: Imagining a Future Where a Spy Could Disappear
entries.summary: In Emily St. John Mandel’s new novel Exit Party, becoming a “ghost” means running afoul of the state. In this excerpt, a secret agent discovers it doesn’t take much.
entries.content:
True diligence is following the improbable path. I read the sentence in a detective novel in childhood, when I was 8 or 9 years old, and then the phrase stayed with me forever after.

For a long time I wrote True Diligence in stylized curly letters on the inside page of every notebook, or sometimes on the front cover. I had notebooks for writing down clues, because even at 9 I wanted to work for the Internal Intelligence Service. What child doesn’t secretly wish to be a spy?

We were terrified and fascinated by Service in equal measure. Service was dark cars moving down the block, men and women in forgettable clothing stopping our parents on the street for brief random interrogations. Service was the force that made people disappear—when I was in the first grade, my friend from across the street climbed into the back of a black car with her parents, and their apartment stood empty for a year before other people moved in—but also Service carried a kind of dark glamour, an aura of power that called to us.

We played Ghosts and Agents all the time, my friends and I, but eventually they drifted off into other interests and I still wanted to be a spy, so after high school I applied successfully to the Service Academy in Los Angeles. I was talented and moved through school quickly, and afterward I was posted to Fillmore, a pretty town about 80 kilometers north of LA. My parents came to visit me there in my first year.

“This is lovely, Ibari,” my mother said, when she stepped off the train. The town made a good first impression. The central station was beautiful, one of those Southern California structures with no serious boundary between indoors and out, a tiled platform that turned into a waiting area with benches, then archways opening out to the street.

My parents had been on the train since Ohio, and they looked worn and dazed, blinking in the relentless sunlight. I was only in my mid-twenties at that point, which is to say I hadn’t thought much about the reality of aging parents, and their haziness was a glimpse into a future where I was the adult and they were confused. I didn’t like it.

“Not a cloud in the sky,” my father said.

“Do we need a taxi?” my mother asked. “I wouldn’t mind walking a bit, stretching my legs.”

“My house is close,” I said. “We can easily walk there if you’d like.”

“Downtown residency permit?” my father asked, and whistled softly.

“What can I say,” I said. “I’ve been well-behaved.”

I’ve spent a long time thinking about the nature of life in a surveillance state, which is perhaps obvious given my work, but there are observations I’ve made that I share with no one, and one of them has to do with the way in a place like this, reality splits into two.

This will seem a bit obvious­—there’s your actual job, which is Service, and then there’s your cover, which is what you tell everyone you do—­but for a long period of my life, at the beginning of my career, there was truth in both versions.

At the Service Academy I’d been trained in espionage and investigation, obviously, in relevant law, in the ins and outs of running down leads, interrogation, documentation, maintaining relationships with confidential informants, etc., but also I’d earned a master’s in urban planning, and this was my cover. As far as my parents and everyone else in my life was concerned, I was an up-­and-­coming academic with a tenure-­track job at the local college. My parents didn’t know I was Service, because no one in my life knew I was Service.

Here was the branching, as I thought of it, the point where one reality split off into another: It was actually true that I was a junior professor in an urban planning department. I’d applied for and earned that position, or so I told myself—­if strings were pulled behind the scenes, that was well above my pay grade—and I took that job seriously. With that being the case, was it really just cover? It was a real job, a real life. When I introduced myself as a college instructor in urban planning, it wasn’t a lie. There was an expansiveness about it. It was like getting to live two lives at once.

But in every version of reality I had an absolutely clean record, no subversion or other crimes of any kind, which had qualified me for a permit to live in an attractive neighborhood close to downtown. My parents and I walked out of the train station and up the hill together, and as an exercise in gratitude I tried to see Central Avenue through their eyes: the double row of palm trees, the century-­old restored movie theater, the candy-­colored awnings above the shops, an overall impression of having been unmoored from time and history sometime around 1965.

“I feel like I’m in a time capsule,” my mother said, and then quickly, “In a good way, I mean. It’s nice here.”

“It is nice,” I said. I­ really did like it here, for the most part. In Fillmore, as in most backwaters without a significant history of subversion, the State operated with a fairly light touch: identity cards, neighborhood permits, and facial recognition technology, like everywhere, but none of the random interrogations and drone surveillance that one might expect in larger cities.

My father took a nap on my couch while my mother and I went for a walk. We took a circuitous route that led us back through downtown. As we turned back onto Central Avenue, my attention was diverted by a scene playing out farther up the block and across the street. A black van had pulled up in front of the florist’s. The shop had been open an hour earlier, but now a crew had gone to work on it: The sign had been painted over, and two men were carting armloads of flowers into the van. The owners—­a couple in their sixties whom I’d been surveilling for some time—­were standing nearby, seemingly in shock. A second van pulled up, and the couple were led inside. They didn’t resist.

In a moment, the two vans were gone, and with them all trace of the business and the business’s owners. The shop was locked and blank now, no merchandise, no signs, the erasure complete. I knew, because I’d reported on this couple to my supervising officer, that they’d criticized the State on social media. They might be sent to prison, or to a black site, but I thought it more likely that they’d be sent to a work camp servicing the massive agricultural operations in the valley, a decade or so of picking strawberries or kale in the sun and sleeping in locked dormitories. People were rarely able to return to their previous life after that. I didn’t expect to see them again.

“This weather’s perfect,” my mother said.

Dinner that night was at a metal table I’d purchased for my backyard grove, as I thought of it: two ancient orange trees and a lemon tree that together formed a canopy. This was my favorite place in the world, and the main reason why I’d bought the house.

“Ibari,” my mother said, “I brought something for you from home.”

Home, for them, was Ohio, where they’d moved from New York when I’d left for the academy. I’d never lived there, and hearing the place called home was obscurely irritating. My mother had brought an ancient canvas tote bag to the table—could this possibly be the same one she’d used for grocery shopping in my childhood in New York?—and from it she pulled a battered old notebook, on which TRUE DILIGENCE and associated curlicues took up the entire front cover.

“Good lord,” I said. “Where did you find that?”

“I was cleaning out the storage unit,” she said, “and thought you might like to have it. What does the phrase mean?”

“True diligence?” I was going for lightness. I felt I’d succeeded. “Just a phrase I liked when I was a little kid. I think I must have seen it on TV or read it in a book somewhere.” If asked, I could have cited the book title, the author, and possibly the page number. Why was I lying about it? Because lying was my job. I pushed this thought down.

“I opened it up,” she said, “before I knew what it was. You should’ve been a detective.”

“Why,” I said, “what’s in it?” She was passing it across the table. I opened it, and for a moment didn’t understand what I was looking at. A timetable? No, the times of day when the neighbor at the apartment building across the street entered or left the building, except it was all only between 4 pm and 6 pm, because that was the time when I was sitting at my desk by the window doing homework, between school and dinner. He came and went a lot during that period, which I’d apparently found suspicious. The heading was straightforward: Times when Andy Commidy (sp?) enters or leaves home, with separate columns for enters and leaves. His schedule was remarkably consistent. I’d started the notebook after my friend across the street had disappeared, I remembered now. I was 7. But all these years later, I couldn’t remember my friend’s name.

“Wow,” I said, “I’d forgotten what a weird kid I was.”

“You should’ve been a detective,” she said again. Could she possibly know? It wasn’t possible, I told myself, but on the other hand, how did I know my mother wasn’t Service too? One of the more exhausting aspects of life in a surveillance state is that anyone can be surveilling you at any time, including the person whom you are yourself surveilling.

“I like the academic life,” I said. “It’s peaceful.”

“Anything you did here would seem peaceful, I’d think,” my father said. “Nice little town.”

“Well, Ibari,” my mother said, and raised her wineglass. “It looks like you’ve found a quiet life in a beautiful place.”

“Here’s to that,” my father said, and I smiled and joined them in sipping wine. Why did that comment bother me so much? She’d meant it kindly. Soon enough they returned to Ohio, and I settled back into the rhythms of my life. I was good at my work, both in Service and at the college. My students seemed to like me well enough, and I enjoyed teaching them. My Service work involved surveillance on a handful of local people, adults much older than me, who’d attended the last pro-democracy demonstrations a decade earlier.

It was easy work, observing their activities, listening to their mind-numbingly boring phone calls, meeting regularly with their next-door neighbors, friends, and colleagues. In my cover life, I liked my colleagues at the college. My home was beautiful. The dating pool was small, but I maximized it by dating both women and men. I collected a few local friends and enjoyed their company.

But in the years that followed my parents’ first visit, my mother’s comment—a quiet life in a beautiful place—stayed with me in a way I didn’t understand. It was like a splinter I could ignore for months at a time. Occasionally, in unexpected moments, I was struck by an uneasy sense that I was living the wrong life, or conducting my life in the same way I checked items off my grocery lists, or doing the wrong thing, or in stasis.

Sometime around my 40th birthday, while my friend Nico was visiting, I broke my glasses. I was picking oranges in the backyard when it happened. I’d taken the glasses off for only a moment, to wipe sweat from my face, but managed to drop them. I stepped back, looking at the ground in the dim greenish light under the orange tree, and heard a quiet snap under my shoe. The nose bridge was broken.

“You got a backup pair?” Nico asked, from the lounge chair. She’d been reading a book.

“In my office at the college,” I said.

“Do you have tape?”

“Probably. Keep reading, I’ve got this.” But all I seemed to have in the house, tape-­wise, was a reflective silver tape that my cousin Anton had left behind on a recent visit, when he’d come for a few days with his 4-­year-­old twins, who were forever immersed in complicated art projects. The tape was very narrow but surprisingly strong. I carefully wound it around the broken section, then the right lens popped out, so I added more tape on the right. The glasses felt secure when I put them on, but the overall look was insane. I was staring in the mirror when the doorbell rang.

“Nice repair job, Ibari,” the UPS driver said. He came around often enough that we were on a first-­name basis. In those days I did a lot of online shopping.

“Thank you. I just stepped on them.”

“Happens to the best of us,” he said, and raised his device close to my face. “Voice?”

“My voice is my passcode,” I said reflexively, and waited, with the driver, for the signature of my voice and the image of my face to match with my address in the UPS system, so that the driver could leave the small package he held, which I thought was probably my new toothbrush. Instead, his device emitted a sharp warning beep.

“Seems like there’s a problem with the face scan,” the driver said.

“Let’s try that again.” He raised the device.

“My voice is my passcode.” The beep came again.

“Try again without the glasses?”

“My glasses have never been a problem,” I said, but took them off anyway. “You’re sure you can’t just leave the package?”

“Without ID verification?” The driver grinned. “I didn’t know you did stand-up. OK, take three?”

“My voice is my passcode,” I said, with the glasses in my hand, and this time the machine produced a melodic chime.

“There you go,” the driver said. “Enjoy the rest of your day.”

I thanked him, and brought the little package in. I felt very strange. It was as if a curtain had been pulled aside, just for a second, and I’d seen the machinery hidden behind it. I’d never ­ really thought about facial recognition systems before, because they were everywhere and always had been, my face recorded and uploaded to a central database several times a day since earliest memory. The question was whether the glasses could thwart any facial recognition software, or if it was just a faulty UPS scanner. I returned to the backyard with a feeling of carrying a dangerous secret. I wanted to test my glasses again.

“Nico,” I said, “you want to go for a walk, maybe get some iced tea downtown?”

Nico smiled. “Your poor glasses,” she said. “Yes, iced tea sounds perfect.”

We walked slowly, in the direction of iced tea. It was a hot day, but the solar fans in the business district created a gentle breeze. There was a man walking a block or so ahead of us. One of the former pro-democracy agitators whom I’d been surveilling. I’d studied him so carefully that I’d have known him anywhere.

“When do you need to be back in LA?” I asked.

“I thought I’d take the 4 o’clock train.” It was still only late morning. As we entered the tea shop, a discreet scanner embedded in the door frame flashed white—Face not found—­but confirmation didn’t come until I reached the front of the line, ordered an iced tea, and stared directly into the screen to pay with credit.

“I’m sorry,” the barista said, and swiveled the screen so I could read the message: Facial recognition error. “I can’t remember the last time this happened.”

“Oh,” I said, “no problem, let’s do fingerprints.” I pressed my right index finger to the screen, and a moment later a green check mark appeared. Nico was studying the muffins.

“I think these glasses are throwing off the scanners,” I said.

Nico went still for just a second, and shook her head. The movement was barely perceptible. She was still looking at the baked goods.

“The muffins here look good,” she said, as if I’d said nothing.

This was when I understood: My friend was Service. I had no doubt that she was who she said she was, which is to say an associate professor in the physics department at UCLA, but also she was something else. It shouldn’t be disappointing, I told myself. A lot of people were Service. I was Service. The barista could be Service. Anyone around you, at any given moment, could be observing and reporting. But was she reporting on me? We were quiet on the walk back to the house. The iced tea tasted like cardboard.

“I’ve never reported on you,” Nico said, when we were close to my house. She spoke so quietly that I barely heard her, and I knew it wasn’t a coincidence that she’d waited until our backs were to the downtown camera array.

“OK.” I felt vastly relieved. I knew that rationally there was no reason to believe her, but all my life I’ve had a sense of intuition, and I felt very strongly that she was telling the truth. And then, because she was my closest friend and she’d taken the risk first: “I’ve never reported on you either,” I said.

She didn’t stop walking, but I heard a slight intake of breath.

“You know,” she said, again very softly, “I think it doesn’t take that much to become a ghost.”

“You’re probably right.” I appreciated the warning. Ghost was slang for a person who ran afoul of the State. A ghost is undesirable. A ghost lives in the shadows. A ghost is not entitled to a home, or health care, or the protections of the law, or a social security number, bank account, credit, or entry into most spaces, because does a ghost even really entirely exist?

entries.title: Vari Electric Standing Desk Review (2026): Form and Value
entries.summary: The Vari Ergo electric standing desk is compact, easy to assemble, affordable, and gently sloped to fit my natural posture and shape.
entries.content:
In my job as a product reviewer, I have learned to fear large boxes. Each one that arrives, whether an office chair or a pellet smoker, might mean anywhere from 20 minutes to multiple hours scratching my head at arcane diagrams, while bent upside down trying to find the right place to put a screw without dropping it.

And so the four-step instruction manual on the Vari Ergo electric standing desk was a source of immense relief. Ever since the Texas-based standing desk company first started rolling out standing desk conversion kits in the early 2010s (then under the name Varidesk), Vari has put a heartening emphasis on ease of assembly. This is an underrated quality, one that goes along way toward forging a good relationship between me and my furniture.

By the time I had the Ergo upright and plugged in, 10 minutes out of the box, my desk and I were pretty much good buddies. It’s a relationship that has continued apace over multiple months of testing.

The Ergo is sturdy, easily (and quietly) adjustable across a broad range of height from 25 to 50 inches, and somewhat elegant in a minimalist way. It doesn’t have any drawers, and I might want better cable management, but the Ergo otherwise covers most every base I need covered from a standing desk.

The Basic Specs

Height range: 25 to 50.5 inches
Desktop sizes: 54 x 26
Memory Presets: Four
Load: 200-pound operational load
Weight: 104 pounds
Warranty: Lifetime

An Affordable, Compact Option

The Ergo’s virtues are quite simple: The desk is sturdy on its T-shaped legs, with minimal wobble. It adjusts easily, with a relatively quiet dual-motor system, across a broad range from 25 inches to 50 inches high. The warranty is for life, at least on manufacturing defects under normal operation.

The desk’s three-stage, T-bottomed legs mean the desk stays stable even at its top height—a problem among some desks in the lower price range, and I’m able to set four different pre-set heights. In practice, this is one more than I even need: I have mine set for seated typing, face height for Zoom calls, and standing height.

entries.title: Clearview AI Is Testing an AI Tool That Would Let Cops Unearth Your Life Online
entries.summary: InquiryIQ, a previously unreported prototype, tested a model from xAI, maker of Grok, to surface associates, social accounts, and other information about people identified through Clearview.
entries.content:
In 2020, face-recognition firm Clearview AI became infamous for scraping more than 3 billion photos from the internet to turn faces into names for police and security professionals. Now the company is experimenting with trawling the web again, this time using AI to potentially help law enforcement fill in the person behind the name—who they are, who they know, where they live, and what they’ve left behind online.

Clearview has quietly built and tested what it describes as an experimental AI “analyst assistant,” WIRED has learned. Called InquiryIQ, the unreleased tool is designed to take details an investigator unearths from a Clearview search and then automatically fan out across the web—opening webpages, analyzing images, and assembling what it finds into a profile containing the possible employers, aliases, associates, and physical characteristics of a person police are investigating.

InquiryIQ’s interface states that supplying age, gender, and race can help the system make “smarter decisions” as it searches, according to code for the tool analyzed by WIRED. One of the models that the company tested to power those decisions comes from SpaceXAI, the Elon Musk company behind Grok. (SpaceX and xAI merged in February.) Musk has pitched Grok as an alternative to supposedly “woke” AI systems, and the chatbot has repeatedly drawn scrutiny for racist, extremist, and inflammatory outputs. It is unclear how SpaceXAI would use those demographic inputs or how they might shape its output, and Clearview declined to speculate.

Experts say InquiryIQ and tools like it could reshape police investigations by compressing days or weeks of detective work into minutes. That speed could help police solve crimes faster, but it also lowers the cost of fishing expeditions, making it practical to scrutinize people police might otherwise never have investigated. And because generative AI can produce different answers from the same starting point, they say, it may be difficult to reconstruct why the system pursued one lead instead of another.

Clearview tells WIRED that InquiryIQ is a prototype that has never been pitched or shipped to customers and is not currently planned for release in its present form. The company also disputes that the tool amounts to an automated investigator. Instead, it describes InquiryIQ as a limited way to automate the web searches detectives already perform. In an interview, CEO Amos Kyler says the SpaceXAI and other model options visible in the interface were included so Clearview’s engineers could compare how different models performed during testing, not so police could choose which model ran the research. “No law enforcement user has ever used it, period,” Kyler says.

WIRED discovered InquiryIQ in files that Clearview’s login page sends to any visitor’s browser before they sign in. It was the same technique WIRED used last month to uncover OS Investigate, an AI-powered search tool being developed by Flock Safety, and to reconstruct a mock-up of its interface from publicly accessible files.

Clearview’s files similarly contain code and thousands of lines of text for its user interface—instructions, warnings, and feature descriptions that show how the company has designed and described InquiryIQ. They do not reveal exactly what happens inside Clearview’s servers, how well the tool works, or who has used it. According to the text, InquiryIQ is built to “automatically discover and enrich personal data from web sources.”

Clearview says the apparent completeness of InquiryIQ’s interface should not be mistaken for a product nearing release. Modern AI tools have made it much faster to build sophisticated prototypes, the company says, and the directive to Clearview’s engineers is to move prototypes along rapidly because it’s now possible to do so.

Founded in 2017, Clearview spent its first years operating largely out of public view. Peter Thiel invested $200,000 that year, and the company soon began signing up police departments and offering free trials around the country. A 2020 HuffPost investigation later detailed founder Hoan Ton-That’s ties to the far right, including a 2016 Republican National Convention dinner with white nationalist Richard Spencer and participation in a private online community populated by far-right activists and extremists. Ton-That later apologized for his past writings.

In 2020, The New York Times revealed that Clearview had scraped more than 3 billion images from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo, and millions of other websites. Overnight, the report transformed the company into one of the country’s most controversial surveillance firms. Tech companies demanded that it stop harvesting their users’ photos; lawsuits and regulatory investigations followed. But Clearview kept scraping. Its database grew from more than 3 billion images in 2020 to what the company now says is well over 70 billion, and Clearview says its technology is used by more than 2,000 law enforcement agencies nationwide.

Ton-That stepped down as CEO in December 2024 and left the board the following spring. Kyler, who became CEO in October last year, joined Clearview as an engineer in 2019 and presents a more deliberate, technical face of the company. Where Clearview’s early years were defined by boundary-pushing, Kyler talks instead about controls, auditing, and oversight.

“The mission today is the same,” Kyler says. But he describes the company’s recent focus as “refinement” and “ensuring that the product hits the kind of expectation of integrity that our customers expect.”

Signals and Noise

For years, Clearview said its job stopped at surfacing possible leads for law enforcement using face recognition. In a 2022 post, Ton-That wrote that it was “up to the investigator to follow those links and do more research to find additional information.” InquiryIQ appears designed to take on some of that work.

As Clearview describes it, InquiryIQ would begin after an investigator has already run a face-recognition search and identified details they consider relevant. Those details can be added to a profile alongside information such as age, gender, race, hair color, and eye color, which the interface says can help the AI make “smarter decisions when running its searches.”

Kyler says InquiryIQ was conceived as a way to test pieces of information an investigator had already identified as potentially relevant. “We looked at it in the form of trying to put together a proposition and then invalidating a proposition,” he says. The system would take a “factoid,” run searches around it, and ask, as Kyler puts it, “Is this related or not?”

The code WIRED reviewed describes InquiryIQ as able to run web and image searches, browse web pages, and use face recognition on photographs it encounters. As the system searches from information supplied by the investigator, it is designed to build what Clearview calls a “Candidate Graph” of possible identities and associates, while filling out the subject’s profile with possible addresses, phone numbers, employers, social media accounts, arrest history, and aliases.

Clearview is not the first company to automate the process of trawling publicly available information. Other intelligence platforms sold to law enforcement, including ShadowDragon’s SocialNet, Penlink’s Tangles, and Fivecast, help investigators uncover aliases and associates and map a person’s digital footprint.

Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a George Washington University law professor who studies AI and policing, describes this kind of automated investigation as “digital rummaging.” “They're basically going to create a profile of you based on all of the random digital clues you left on the internet,” he explains. In practice, that means gathering scattered bits of information that once lived in separate places but were difficult to connect.

Woodrow Hartzog, a Boston University privacy scholar, argues that the labor of investigative work once served as a practical check on surveillance. By vastly reducing the labor required to investigate a person, tools like InquiryIQ also eliminate those checks. “The privacy protections we have in place right now were mainly built in a world that assumed a certain amount of friction in the ability of governments to collect information about people,” he says. “There are a lot of rules we never had just because we never needed them—because there were these practical barriers to following everyone around.”

When an InquiryIQ search is finished, the interface is designed to present the officer with the identities, connections, and other details the system has surfaced, which the officer can accept or reject before they are added to the profile. Clearview warns that automatically generated demographic, social media, and arrest data “may or may not be accurate.” Before accepting any finding, the officer must attest that they independently verified it.

Got a Tip?
Do you have information about Clearview AI that you'd like to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at dmehro.89.

Kyler says that human review is central to Clearview’s design. The system is meant to surface possible leads, not determine what is true, he says. “That’s the job of an analyst—to evaluate what’s true, what’s not; what’s noise, what’s reality.”

“A human in the loop is a little bit of a cold comfort,” Hartzog says. Over time, investigators can defer to automated systems until the person checking the machine becomes “a sort of rubber stamp.”

For example, in United States v. Sant, a Minnesota case involving undercover Homeland Security Investigations agents and surveillance of political activists, defense lawyers obtained a Clearview report drawing matches from roughly 15 years of protest photography. Every result was stamped "Accepted by Guy Gino," including one Clearview itself labeled "A Less Likely Result"—which, the report's footnote notes, can only be exported if a user accepts it. Defense attorneys allege the report swept in photos of an entirely different man, his pregnant wife, and young daughter. (There is no evidence InquiryIQ was used in the case.)

Pitfalls and Silver Linings

In the prototype WIRED reviewed, what InquiryIQ returned could vary depending on which model was selected. Its interface includes a control for choosing the model that runs the research and lists xAI and Amazon Bedrock, a platform for accessing models built by other companies.

In 2025, what xAI said was an unauthorized change to Grok’s system prompt caused the chatbot to inject claims about a supposed “white genocide” in South Africa into unrelated conversations. Less than a month later, after another change to its instructions, Grok produced antisemitic posts and praise for Adolf Hitler. SpaceXAI did not respond to a request for comment.

“A hallucination-prone chatbot would not be trusted as an informant under any other regular circumstances,” says Michael Price, litigation director of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers’ Fourth Amendment Center, referring specifically to information police rely on to establish probable cause in court. “This person just told me to go eat rocks and drink bleach. And they’re going to be the basis for probable cause?”

Price, who helped litigate Chatrie v. United States, the landmark Supreme Court case over geofence warrants, argues that concerns around the reliability of generative AI tools extends beyond Grok. AI models are trained on material pulled from the internet, including, he says, “uninformed posts, conspiracy theories, all of the prejudices that sadly seem to go along with the internet.”

Kyler says the apparent model selector is for internal testing and not so police could choose which model to use for their research. He insists that InquiryIQ’s output, like everything Clearview surfaces, would be treated as information for investigators to evaluate, with human analysts responsible for deciding what constitutes a real lead. The company’s interest is to “help generate a lead that leads to ground truth,” he says. “That leads to reality.”

Clearview says it is continuously evaluating a wide variety of available large language models and has not assessed the suitability of any of them for InquiryIQ.

In a statement, Amazon says that AWS is not involved in the development of InquiryIQ and that customers are responsible for ensuring they comply with the company’s terms and policies, including our acceptable use policy and responsible AI policy, as well as any third-party provider's terms. The company also stated that it does not have service-specific terms that prevent law enforcement from using Amazon Bedrock.

In spite of the risks of tools like InquiryIQ, Ferguson sees potential upside to AI-assisted investigations. They could, for example, leave a clearer record of how police arrived at a suspect than traditional detective work does. Officers routinely search databases, discard leads, and follow hunches without documenting every step, he explains. An AI system that preserved its prompts, searches, model choices, and investigative paths could make that process easier to audit.

“It’s a silver lining in an otherwise potentially fraught and disruptive change,” Ferguson says.

Ferguson’s optimism is tempered, however, by 16 years of watching police technology get deployed before agencies work out how it should be governed. “I’m a cynic because I’ve seen this happen every single time,” Ferguson says. “It’s another new technology, the same playbook.”

entries.title: A Teen Girl’s Death Is Prompting Calls to Ban Choking in Porn
entries.summary: Despite the many health risks, sexual strangulation has become popular among young people—with some experts blaming adult content for normalizing it.
entries.content:
An Australian teenage girl’s death, suspected to be preceded by consensual “choking” during sex, has renewed calls to ban showing the act in porn.

This latest tragedy, reportedly believed to involve sexual strangulation, comes just months after the UK banned porn showing the practice. But despite all the noise, most people still aren’t aware of just how dangerous the trend is.

Sexual strangulation or “choking” during sex, as it’s referred to colloquially, has become wildly popular—especially among adults aged 18 to 35, despite the risk of severe injury, brain damage, and even death. Some researchers argue that porn is to blame for that normalization, but members of the adult industry say that banning depictions of choking won’t stop this kind of content from flourishing or serve as the kind of sex education and media literacy the public sorely needs.

“With the misinformation that’s out there, especially online, many people do think that maybe at lighter pressures they might be ‘safe,’ and that’s not the case,” says Debby Herbenick, a professor at the Indiana University School of Public Health and one of the leading researchers on sexual strangulation. Herbenick cautions that applying sustained pressure to the front and sides of the throat—via your hands, an object, or otherwise—can lead to blood clots and stroke, tears in the carotid arteries, vision impairment, and cumulative brain injuries.

“It’s these things that we wouldn’t even notice,” she says. “Those tiny, incremental changes in your vision, or your brain, or so on.”

Or, in the most extreme cases, death. Pressing on the front of the throat can lead to airway collapse, Herbenick says. Two weeks ago, a 16-year-old girl in Sydney passed out after authorities believe she was strangled by her equally young partner during sex. She died after being taken to a local hospital in critical condition, and the investigation is ongoing. It’s unknown what her exact injuries were.

The Australian Social Services Minister has since said the government is “very seriously” looking at efforts to ban pornographic depictions of choking in sex, in line with the country’s recently passed age-verification laws that ban social media for children under the age of 16. But critics of these social media bans say they don’t actually work and make it harder for teens to access news and information they need, including sex education around the dangers of choking and strangulation.

The data regarding rates of young people choking and being choked during sex can appear staggering. In Herbenick’s 2021 survey of nearly 5,000 college students in the US, 58 percent of women had been choked during sex and a quarter had been first choked by age 17. Researchers in Australia similarly found rates of around half of people aged 18 to 35 engaging in the practice. Herbenick found that women are usually the ones being choked by men during heterosexual sex and that sexual and gender minorities are also more likely to be choked during sex.

“There are other people who say ‘I asked them to choke me or I said it was OK, but then they really pushed past my limits or it was a lot harder than I expected, or I asked them to stop and they didn’t,’” Herbenick says. She also says that while some young men enjoy the act, others “tell us that they don’t want to be choking their partners, but they think they’re supposed to, or they get asked all the time.”

Most of the self-reported occurrences of sexual strangulation among US college students Herbenick surveyed were described as consensual, but when choking is nonconsensual, it can be even more dangerous. In fact, strangulation is one of the strongest predictors for murder in an abusive relationship.

It’s important to distinguish between the different types of intimate partner strangulation: as a form of abuse, nonconsensual introduction of strangulation into what may have started as a consensual hookup, fully consensual choking, and fictional depictions of choking, like what is usually happening in legal pornography and television. But with the exception of staged or implied choking (like placing a hand over a partner’s neck without actually applying pressure), all of these kinds of strangulation carry major and even deadly health risks for the person on the receiving end.

Clare McGlynn, a law professor at Durham University whose work has contributed to pornography regulation in the UK for 20 years, says the amount of porn involving strangulation has risen over the past few decades and corresponds with an increase in children viewing strangulation content.

“If you ask young people, ‘Where do you get your ideas for sex or sexual activity?’ they say ‘porn.’ And you think, ‘Well, yeah, of course you do,’” McGlynn says. “I think its ubiquity in porn does mean that’s why we see large numbers of young people engaging in this practice consensually, because they think through scripts they’ve seen in mainstream porn that it’s normal, it’s expected.”

The UK’s recent ban on porn showing strangulation or suffocation falls under the country’s Online Safety Act, which requires social media platforms, search engines, and other web services to proactively remove illegal material and employ controversial age-verification measures. According to McGlynn, the strangulation ban was adopted in April but hasn’t been implemented or enforced yet, meaning the government has yet to take action against any companies or individuals.

“The platforms aren’t going to act in and of themselves,” she says. “They’re only going to act if they think the regulator is going to take action against them.”

McGlynn believes that within a few years of the ban on strangulation in porn actually being enforced, a new generation of young people may grow up without seeing choking as a standard part of sex. It’s an optimistic view—one that isn’t shared by everyone.

Cherie DeVille, a well-known pornographic actress, points to the fallout from age-verification laws—requiring proof of age to access adult content—as an example of the futility of banning porn. Consumers can simply use VPNs to get around local laws and turn to the unregulated world of sexually explicit content, often hosted by foreign platforms that don’t comply with any of the laws that major companies are forced to obey.

DeVille, who was a physical therapist prior to entering the adult film industry, describes how talent liaisons assist in the negotiation of what is allowed in specific scenes before filming, including choking, which she says never involves putting actual pressure on the trachea.

Pornhub echoed its consent policy for performers in an email statement to WIRED, writing, “We can be confident that the acts that appear in our content are completely consensual, unlike other platforms that don't have the same consent requirements.” Meanwhile, adult creators on OnlyFans are wary of posting anything involving choking after the service was forced to clamp down on most hardcore content in 2021 to avoid banks freezing payments. (OnlyFans didn’t respond to a request for comment about whether choking and sexual strangulation are technically banned on the platform.)

While Herbenick says that young men are more likely to learn about sexual strangulation from porn, young women are more likely to learn about it from memes, mainstream entertainment, or even erotic fanfiction about One Direction. HBO director Sam Levinson featured it in early episodes of Euphoria and The Idol. It was the opener to a chart-topping Jack Harlow song, where he crooned about choking a woman but not being a “killer.”

“Porn is an appealing boogeyman to say we can stop this by regulating this very specific type of speech, despite the fact that this is ubiquitous throughout culture,” says Mike Stabile, the director of public policy for the Free Speech Coalition, which is the nonprofit trade association for the US adult industry. “The solution is education. The solution is to talk about consent rather than try and find a singular cause that, if you were able to censor it, will solve the problem.”

Herbenick agrees about education. She says one of the biggest cultural changes we need to make is for parents to talk to their kids and teenagers about the dangers of strangulation and the type of messaging they’re consuming about choking during sex—whether it’s in porn or the Billboard Hot 100.

entries.title: Want to Get Off Your Phone? Mina Kimes Suggests Having a Baby
entries.summary: “I think that's been the most helpful thing,” says the ESPN journalist. “So there you go, Zoomers. There's a reason to have children.”
entries.content:
As an NFL analyst and podcast host, Mina Kimes consumes a lot of news online, but ask her to spend more than 15 minutes on “any social media platform” and you might have a problem. “It's like simultaneously pouring molasses into your brain and lighting it on fire,” she says.

These days, a declaration of social media hatred isn’t exactly a hot tech take. But Kimes is full of those too. For one, she thinks FaceTiming anyone outside of your family is “insane behavior.” She also prefers to keep her phone perpetually unlocked and practices inbox zero like it’s a religion. And she loves finding corners of the internet where she can see men encouraging other men.

For our latest User Behavior, Kimes tells WIRED all about her favorite heartwarming subreddits, her “hijacked” Spotify Wrapped, and her folder of memes.

I just got it replaced because I cracked the screen with my car. I was resting it on the roof and it slid down as I was opening the trunk, and it was a real crime scene. When you bring a cracked phone to an Apple store, you know that they've seen everything, but you still feel deeply ashamed. Usually I'm pretty good about not cracking it, which is amazing because I have a toddler who likes to drop it and throw it and stuff. I got it replaced, and I didn't get the new one because I like this model.

It’s dying on me a little bit. The fan, at inappropriate times, starts making noises like an air-conditioning unit circa 1985. It's like a radiator whistle. And it's one of those things where you start developing weird habits and superstitions. I'm like, “Maybe if I tilt it this way and don't plug it in and don't run too many things, it'll be fine. It won't make noises.” But the truth is, I probably should just get it serviced or replaced.

I actually don't have it set up to show me, which sounds a little bit like the meme “I pretend I do not see it,” but I would estimate it's probably around four hours a day. This is going to sound insane, but I have my phone set to where it doesn't lock because I don't like seeing a clock at night. So my way of hiding that information was to just have my phone not lock. When I did that, I realized it would register as a very high screen time, but I'm not actually on my phone. I realized the screen-time feature was kind of functionally useless for me.

To be honest, I don't feel bad about screen time generally, because I use my phone for reading the news, studying, looking at tape, preparing for work, answering emails. None of that stuff bothers me. However, I would feel terrible if I saw how much time I spend on social media. I think those things kind of get conflated a little bit when we think about screen time and phones. At least for me, I think there's a pretty big distinction.

I feel bad when I spend more than 15 minutes on any social media platform, because it's like simultaneously pouring molasses into your brain and lighting it on fire. And I have very much noticed a very pronounced and obvious correlation between my happiness and how much time in any given day I spend on social media in particular.

On my phone, I have Instagram, Reddit, and Bluesky. But I've taken stuff off. It's a little bit tricky because when I post clips or promote my podcast or YouTube or the various things I do at ESPN, I often do that on my phone, which makes it hard to eliminate them. But something I'll do is when I'm done, I'll just log out immediately: post, log out, walk away.

The best way to digital detox is to have a kid, because when I spend time with him I'm just not on my phone by necessity. I think that's been the most helpful thing. So there you go, Zoomers. There's a reason to have children. And honestly, I do notice when I spend a day with him, whether it's hiking or at the beach, and I'm not on my phone, I'm infinitely happier at the end of the day than any other day in my life.

I primarily use Spotify. The data is completely cooked because of the aforementioned 3-year-old. So when they do Spotify Wrapped, I swear to God, it used to be cool, but now it's been hijacked by Raffi, Elmo, Ms. Rachel, Mickey Mouse. My son is really into Mickey’s Countdown lately. I feel like 99 percent of my Spotify listening now is just atrocious kids' music. Raffi's the GOAT though. I don't want to lump him in with some of the people that I mentioned. Raffi stands alone.

This is probably the thing where you're going to learn the most about me. Zero unread emails and inbox 10 and under is how I live my life. It's such an important part of how I work and get stuff done.

The number one thing I should lead with is, for a litany of reasons, I just do not let communication build up, which can be difficult, because I subscribe to a couple newsletters, and I won't archive them until I've either read them or scanned them. But I can't get to work until I feel like my mind is clear, and my mind isn't clear if my inbox isn't clear. I think it's probably something I inherited from my dad, who was an Air Force major, and from a very young age he taught me the importance of to-do lists, which I also abide by. Sometimes, on a to-do list, I’ll set aside half an hour or whatever to get my inbox back down to sub-10.

Sometimes that means that when I reply to emails, my response is a fraction of the email that was sent to me. And I think people feel social pressure to match an email with a commensurate email. To live the Inbox 10 lifestyle, you cannot abide by that pressure.

Same thinking, same principle, same possible OCD.

I FaceTimed with my brother, who's on vacation with his family in Delaware at the moment. I'm not a big FaceTimer. And candidly, I feel like FaceTiming someone who is outside of your family is insane behavior. But that's another way in which having a child changed how I use technology, I suppose, because it really is a wonderful way for young children to see distant relatives and communicate with them.

I recently, and I'm very late to this, started strength training at a gym for the first time in my life. For my entire life, I've only gone to the gym to run. And now I'm just learning what all these machines do and how to use them. But I'm like a child. I'm a total neophyte in this world. I have a trainer, but I've also found it’s a really encouraging and fun section of the internet.

It's a picture of my son standing next to a tower he built in his room. I feel like at this point, 95 percent of the photos on my phone are of my son. It's kind of sad; you can see the exact point where we had him because it used to be all pictures of my dog, and then it just completely switches to pictures of my son.

I can’t even remember what I was using it as a meme for, but I clearly needed that screenshot to use as a meme.

I don't really use LLMs. If I do, it's for either menial household questions or basic search. And I only use it for search because search is now useless due to AI.

I've read and listened to a lot of people talk about how it's revolutionized their workflow, and they're training agents to make appointments and they're building these elaborate meal plans. And to me, that doesn't sound interesting. That just sounds exhausting. We have this phrase in football called “looking for work,” when a player on the field is looking for work—looking for someone to block, for example. And I just think about that whenever I hear those stories. It just sounds like you're looking for work.

Also, just fucking do it yourself. It’s not that hard to make a fucking restaurant reservation.

Whether you use vertical cry or laugh cry is a strong divide between different types of people.

I post everywhere to try and get my work out there and get it seen and read. But I would say the one that I use the most is Bluesky. While it has its flaws, there's definitely the occasional sports ball person in my mentions. I’ve found the interactions on there are the most like interactions I have with people in the real world, which is a rarity on the social internet these days.

Everyone says Twitter, right? Which is a bummer because it used to be really fun and essential for news. When breaking news was happening, it was a place you'd go to get on-the-ground impressions. You could meet friends, you could find new writers and comedians, and all of that feels lost just because Elon completely killed the vibe. And I say that because obviously he's done things far more serious in terms of poisoning the discourse, and the place is a cesspool for racism and misogyny and misinformation, but it's also just, like, a terrible fucking hang. Everyone either seems miserable or is determined to make other people miserable.

I am a dedicated Times reader. I know it has its pluses and minuses. I read the Times daily newsletter every day. I find it's generally a pretty good way to stay informed, and there's still really good journalism. There's another newsletter I love for people in Los Angeles called L.A. Material that I've really enjoyed, just getting more local news, which seems to be where things are headed newswise.

Whenever I'm watching a TV show, I do like to read the subreddits, whether it's Love Island or Silo. I find that the conversations about the TV shows are best there. I also like some of the popular ones that are general interest, like r/mildlyinteresting or r/food.

Sometimes the algorithm on the main feed surfaces subreddits for me that I'm intrigued by. One thing, this is going to sound so weird, is the reddit for bald people, r/bald. It's guys, and women, posting pictures of themselves, asking the community if it's time to “come home,” as they call it: shave their heads. Or people who have done it and are asking what people think. And then it's thousands of people being like, "You look amazing. Congrats, king." And I just love that. I love that sort of encouraging corner of the internet.

I got this Bose Bluetooth speaker as a giveaway at some event I did. It has completely made car rides with my kids so much easier, because he holds it and he feels like he has control over the music. I play music out of there instead of my car now, and he loves it. And he’s now so much more willing to take long car rides because of it.

I have a folder. It's a lot of Simpsons stuff just because I'm a Simpsons fanatic. J.R. Smith. I haven't thought about that one in a while. That's a good one. Oh, I love the one of Marge Simpson dancing. I don't even know how to describe that. There’s also the José Mourinho “I prefer not to speak. If I speak, I am in big trouble.” It's a sports thing.

Anything I want to say, I'll just say it.

Especially when I was a writer and business journalist, but even afterwards, I loved Google Reader as a way to organize news articles and feel like I got through them. It was just a great interface. I use Feedly now, which is pretty good to read news, but doesn't quite hit like Google Reader used to hit.

I have recently gotten into trivia after competing on Celebrity Jeopardy and getting introduced to that world a bit. I started to get more into trivia and studying it and tactics. And something I do now at night is just try to learn as much as I can about random topics and then make flashcards.

So last night I made a bunch of flashcards about the Chinese dynasties: Han dynasty, Tang dynasty, Song dynasty.

entries.title: A Satellite Falling Out of Orbit Embarks on Its Final Mission
entries.summary: Before reentering our atmosphere, the telescopes onboard NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory have been restarted to take their last observations.
entries.content:
NASA has carried out some notable rescue missions over the past few years, including bringing home the astronauts stranded on the International Space Station last year. More recently, the agency sent up a probe in hopes of saving the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a satellite first launched in 2004 that began falling out of our planet’s orbit.

The plan was for robotic arms on the probe, known as LINK, to grab onto the aging satellite and—with a powerful set of thrusters—drag the observatory back into position. The rescue robot was launched into space this past July but soon after suffered issues with its altitude systems, a key set of controls for moving in space. The mission had to be canceled.

“Swift wasn't designed to be serviced,” Ghonhee Lee—CEO of Katalyst Space, the company that developed LINK—stated just before the probe’s launch. And as Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s astrophysics division, also noted at the time, this was “a high-risk, high-reward mission.”

Now, Swift will continue sinking. Like all low-orbit satellites, the observatory experiences air resistance from Earth’s upper atmosphere, causing it to gradually descend. Originally, scientists predicted the telescopes might not reach critical depths until 2030, but in recent years, intense solar activity has caused the Earth’s atmosphere to expand, increasing drag. Swift is expected to reenter the atmosphere as soon as the end of this year, though it may still capture some fascinating information about our cosmos before burning up on its descent.

The satellite has been NASA’s eyes on some of the most explosive and short-lived phenomena in the universe. Equipped with three primary telescopes, it’s capable of observing multiple wavelengths, including visible light, ultraviolet, x-rays, and gamma rays. Over 21 years, this has made the observatory indispensable for recording and alerting ground teams about supernovas, gamma-ray bursts, and black holes shredding stars.

The Swift operations team has announced a plan to conduct as many observations as possible during the remaining lifetime. Prior to the rescue mission, the observatory had shut down its telescopes to conserve power, to keep its solar panels oriented, and to minimize air resistance.

But shortly after the rescue mission was abandoned, two of the three telescopes aboard were successfully restarted, and the x-ray telescope captured images of the Tycho supernova remnant, located approximately 13,000 light-years away. Adjustments are also underway for the Burst Alert Telescope, which is still powered down, with the goal of resuming observations within a few weeks.

Once Swift’s altitude falls below 185 miles above the Earth’s surface, operating the telescopes becomes increasingly challenging, and its descent will further accelerate. But researchers are looking forward to what else it might capture before finally expiring.

This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

entries.title: Our Favorite GoPro 360 Camera Is Now 40 Percent Off
entries.summary: The GoPro Max 2 is almost half off at Amazon and other retailers, along with other great action camera deals.
entries.content:
360 cameras use two lenses to simultaneously record everything happening around you, then stitch it together with software. That means you never miss that shot, but because there are essentially two cameras in one, they are more expensive than their action-camera cousins. Right now, though, you can grab my top-pick 360 camera, the GoPro Max 2, for 40 percent off ($299).

The GoPro Max 2 (7/10 WIRED Recommends) is my favorite 360 camera, and that’s still true even with the release of the new Insta360 X6. The X6 is more versatile—it can serve double duty as an action camera and 360 camera better than the Max 2—but judged purely on video quality, I prefer the Max 2. And at this price, you can grab the Max 2 and a GoPro Hero 13 for just $30 more than the X6.

The Max 2’s dual 14-mm (35-mm equivalent) lenses each record to a 1/2.3-inch chip, yielding what GoPro calls “True 8K” video. The large sensors provide sharper, clearer footage than other 360 cameras, and advanced users can record 10-bit color in log for greater flexibility in post-production color grading. Don't want to futz with log video? That’s no problem, as GoPro’s natural-looking color rendition in the default color profile is still the best I’ve tested.

Sharing the same triple mounting system as other GoPros, the Max 2 uses folding fingers, a tripod hole, or a magnetic system. This means you can mount the Max 2 just about anywhere. It also has the simplest lens-cover replacement process if you scratch it (I’ve been using mine for a year now and have no scratches, but it’s nice to know you can easily fix any).

As an action camera, you get all the usual GoPro video modes, including HyperSmooth video stabilization, horizon leveling, TimeWarp time-lapse-style video, and more. The Max 2’s one shortcoming is audio recording quality—it’s not the best. The easiest fix is to get a Bluetooth mic, which you can then pair with the camera. Check out the deal on the DJI Mic 3 below.

entries.title: Trump Probably Won't Give $5,000 to Every American if Republicans Win the Midterms
entries.summary: The eyebrow-raising proposal, delivered during the president’s speech at the midterm convention, would cost $1.2 trillion and would need congressional approval.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday said that he would pay $5,000 to every American if Republicans retained control of the US House and Senate in the midterm elections, seemingly in an effort to incentivize votes for his party.

“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate,” Trump said, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”

“That alone should win the midterms,” he added.

The outlandish remarks came midway through Trump’s at times freewheeling speech at the Republican midterm convention the GOP is holding in Texas, as part of an effort to drive turnout among Trump’s base this November, and were quickly shot down as unaffordable.

It’s unclear whether the “Trump Dividend”, as he’s calling it, was a serious proposal or an attempt to galvanize the president’s base to turn out on election day, after he also previously promised payouts like a $5,000 “DOGE dividend” or a $2,000-per-person tariff check—neither of which has happened. Any attempt to make real on the offer would need congressional approval.

Vice president JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s offer in an interview following the speech, saying it wouldn’t go to wealthy Americans, but also suggested it could be paid for by US tariff revenues. “A one-time payment of this size would wipe out about a decade’s tariff revenue at current tariff levels,” wrote Erica York, senior economist at the Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy, on X.

Responding to a Fox News question that “critics will say the president is bribing voters and he's bankrupting the country”, Vance said: “Tariffs have generated a lot of revenues. The president is saying, if you keep us in power, then you will share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we are creating.”

The rough total cost of paying out $5,000 to about 240 million adults in the US would amount to $1.2 trillion, a price tag that exceeds the roughly $284 billion in gross customs revenue collected between January 2025 and June 2026, according to the University of Pennsylvania.

The shortfall would be even greater after accounting for tariff refunds the Trump administration is compelled to pay after the US Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump had unlawfully imposed tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977.

Following orders from the Court of International Trade, the administration has started to refund some of the $160 billion collected from tariffs, plus interest, which is accruing at an estimated rate of about $650 million per month.

After accounting for refunds, the administration’s net revenue from tariffs will come out to roughly $118 billion, meaning Trump would need to have Congress approve an additional $1.08 trillion, on top of the president’s proposed $1.86 trillion discretionary budget request for fiscal year 2027.

The principal concern for the Republican National Committee has been that the midterm elections will be decided in large part by voter turnout, which could be depressed for Republicans because Trump will not be on the ballot.
